questions.question: A projectile is a body moving under the influence of:
questions.explanation: A projectile is any body that is given an initial velocity and then moves under the influence of gravity alone (neglecting air resistance). The only force acting on it after projection is its weight, which gives it a downward acceleration of g. Air resistance, magnetic force, and friction are not the defining influences for ideal projectile motion.

questions.question: Neglecting air resistance, the path of a projectile is:
questions.explanation: In the absence of air resistance, the horizontal motion is uniform (constant velocity) and the vertical motion is uniformly accelerated (due to gravity). Combining these gives a parabolic trajectory. The equation of the path is y = x tan θ − gx²/(2u² cos²θ), which is a parabola.

questions.question: The horizontal component of a projectile's velocity is:
questions.explanation: If a projectile is launched with initial speed u at an angle θ to the horizontal, its initial velocity can be resolved into two components. The horizontal component is u cos θ, which remains constant throughout the motion (since there is no horizontal acceleration).

questions.question: The vertical component of a projectile's velocity is:
questions.explanation: The vertical component of the initial velocity is u sin θ. This component changes with time due to the downward acceleration of gravity: vy = u sin θ − gt.

questions.question: At the maximum height, the vertical component of velocity is:
questions.explanation: At the highest point of its trajectory, the projectile momentarily stops moving upward, so its vertical velocity becomes zero. The horizontal velocity, however, remains u cos θ.

questions.question: At the maximum height, the acceleration of a projectile is:
questions.explanation: The acceleration of a projectile is always g downward (towards the centre of the Earth) throughout its flight, including at the maximum height. The horizontal acceleration is zero.

questions.question: The time to reach maximum height is:
questions.explanation: At maximum height, the vertical velocity is zero. Using vy = u sin θ − gt, set vy = 0: 0 = u sin θ − gt ⇒ t = u sin θ / g.

questions.question: The total time of flight on level ground is:
questions.explanation: For a projectile launched and landing at the same height, the time of flight is twice the time to reach maximum height: T = 2u sin θ / g.

questions.question: The maximum height reached is:
questions.explanation: Using vy² = (u sin θ)² − 2gH, with vy = 0 at maximum height: 0 = u² sin² θ − 2gH ⇒ H = u² sin² θ / (2g).

questions.question: The horizontal range on level ground is:
questions.explanation: Range R = horizontal velocity × time of flight = (u cos θ) × (2u sin θ / g) = u² (2 sin θ cos θ) / g = u² sin 2θ / g.

questions.question: The range of a projectile is maximum when the angle of projection is:
questions.explanation: Range R = u² sin 2θ / g. This is maximum when sin 2θ = 1, i.e., 2θ = 90° ⇒ θ = 45°.

questions.question: Two angles of projection give the same range if they are:
questions.explanation: Since R = u² sin 2θ / g, the range is the same for angles θ and (90° − θ), because sin 2(90° − θ) = sin(180° − 2θ) = sin 2θ. Such angles are complementary.

questions.question: Which pair of angles gives the same range for the same initial speed?
questions.explanation: Complementary angles give the same range. 20° and 70° add up to 90°, so they are complementary. Hence they give the same range.

questions.question: A projectile launched horizontally from a height h has initial vertical velocity:
questions.explanation: When a projectile is launched horizontally, its initial velocity is entirely horizontal, so the initial vertical velocity is zero. It then accelerates downward under gravity.

questions.question: A body projected horizontally from a height h reaches the ground in time:
questions.explanation: For vertical motion, initial vertical velocity is zero. Using h = ½gt²: t = √(2h/g).

In question 16, the horizontal distance covered is:
questions.explanation: Horizontal distance = horizontal velocity × time = 15 m/s × 2 s = 30 m.

questions.question: A projectile is launched with speed u at angle θ. Its horizontal velocity at any time t is:
questions.explanation: The horizontal component of velocity remains constant throughout the flight (no horizontal acceleration), so it is always u cos θ.

questions.question: Its vertical velocity at any time t is:
questions.explanation: The vertical velocity changes due to gravity: vy = u sin θ − gt.

questions.question: The speed of a projectile at its maximum height is:
questions.explanation: At maximum height, the vertical velocity is zero, so the speed is solely the horizontal component: u cos θ.

questions.question: A projectile is fired at 20 m/s at 30° to the horizontal. Its initial vertical component is:
questions.explanation: Vertical component = u sin θ = 20 × sin 30° = 20 × 0.5 = 10 m/s.

questions.question: In question 21, its initial horizontal component is:
questions.explanation: Horizontal component = u cos θ = 20 × cos 30° = 20 × (√3/2) ≈ 17.3 m/s.

questions.question: In question 21, the time of flight is [g = 10 m/s²]:
questions.explanation: Time of flight T = 2u sin θ / g = (2 × 20 × 0.5)/10 = 20/10 = 2 s.

The horizontal acceleration of a projectile, neglecting air resistance, is:
questions.explanation: There is no horizontal force acting on the projectile (neglecting air resistance), so the horizontal acceleration is zero.

questions.question: The vertical acceleration of a projectile is:
questions.explanation: The only force is gravity, which acts downward, so the vertical acceleration is g downward.

questions.question: At the highest point of its path, the velocity and acceleration of a projectile are:
questions.explanation: At maximum height, velocity is horizontal (u cos θ) and acceleration is vertical downward (g). Therefore they are perpendicular.

questions.question: A projectile has maximum range when sin 2θ equals:
questions.explanation: Range R = u² sin 2θ / g. For maximum range, sin 2θ must be maximum, i.e., sin 2θ = 1.

questions.question: For a given initial speed, the maximum height is greatest when the angle of projection is:
questions.explanation: Maximum height H = u² sin² θ / (2g). This is maximum when sin θ is maximum, i.e., θ = 90°.

questions.question: For a given initial speed, the time of flight is greatest when the angle of projection is:
questions.explanation: Time of flight T = 2u sin θ / g. This is maximum when sin θ is maximum, i.e., θ = 90°.

questions.question: A projectile's horizontal range is zero when projected at:
questions.explanation: Range R = u² sin 2θ / g. If θ = 0°, sin 0° = 0, so range is zero (projectile moves horizontally along the ground).

questions.question: A projectile's horizontal range is zero when projected at:
questions.explanation: If θ = 90°, sin 180° = 0, so range is zero (projectile goes straight up and comes back down).

questions.question: The trajectory of a projectile is represented by:
options: y = x tan θ − gx²/(2u² cos² θ)
questions.explanation: Eliminating t from x = u cos θ t and y = u sin θ t − ½gt² gives the trajectory equation: y = x tan θ − gx²/(2u² cos² θ).

questions.question: A ball is thrown vertically upwards. Its motion is:
questions.explanation: A ball thrown vertically upwards is a special case of projectile motion with θ = 90°. It moves under gravity alone.

questions.question: A projectile is fired at 60° with speed 30 m/s. Its time to maximum height is [g = 10 m/s²]:
questions.explanation: Time to max height t = u sin θ / g = (30 × sin 60°)/10 = (30 × 0.866)/10 ≈ 2.6 s.

The component of velocity that remains constant throughout projectile motion is:
questions.explanation: The horizontal component of velocity remains constant because there is no horizontal acceleration (neglecting air resistance).

questions.question: A projectile is launched at an angle θ. Its kinetic energy at maximum height is:
questions.explanation: At maximum height, the speed is u cos θ. So kinetic energy = ½m(u cos θ)² = ½m u² cos² θ.

questions.question: Its potential energy at maximum height is:
questions.explanation: Potential energy at maximum height = mgh, where h is the maximum height. So mgh.

questions.question: The relation between range R and maximum height H for a projectile is:
questions.explanation: From R = u² sin 2θ / g and H = u² sin² θ / (2g), eliminating u² gives H = R tan θ / 4.

questions.question: For a projectile launched at 45°, the maximum height H and range R are related by:
questions.explanation: At θ = 45°, tan θ = 1. Using H = R tan θ / 4 gives H = R/4, so R = 4H.

questions.question: A projectile has the same range for angles 30° and:
questions.explanation: Complementary angles give same range. 30° and 60° are complementary (30° + 60° = 90°).

questions.question: A projectile is thrown at 10 m/s horizontally from a 45 m high cliff. Time to hit ground is [g = 10 m/s²]:
questions.explanation: Vertical motion: h = ½gt² ⇒ 45 = ½ × 10 × t² ⇒ t² = 9 ⇒ t = 3 s.

questions.question: In question 47, horizontal distance from cliff base is:
questions.explanation: Horizontal distance = horizontal speed × time = 10 m/s × 3 s = 30 m.

questions.question: At maximum height, the vertical component of velocity is zero, but the horizontal component is:
questions.explanation: At maximum height, only the vertical velocity is zero. The horizontal velocity remains u cos θ.

questions.question: The acceleration of a projectile at the highest point is:
questions.explanation: The acceleration due to gravity is always g downward, regardless of the position of the projectile.
